headline: Skipped the chunk grounds, ran the sled to Wilmington's east wall — three yellowfin and a marlin release for eight hours of trolling
subhead: The white marlin bite is building right on schedule, and the yellowfin are still holding tight to the same warm seam we've been fishing since July.
body_markdown:
Tuesday morning I had a decision to make at the dock, and it wasn't a hard one. Chunking had been solid on and off over the canyon's inshore lip, but the fuel burn to sit and soak butterflied bunker for eight hours only pays off if the fish are stacked and eating consistently — and the reports coming off that structure had been more "a few here and there" than a real pile. So I loaded the spread, topped off the tanks, and made the run out to Wilmington's east wall instead, working the 100-fathom break around 38°34' N, 73°58' W where the canyon starts to fall off hard into the deep. If I'm burning that much diesel, I want to be trolling water that's actually holding a temperature edge, not guessing.

And it was there. The warm-water eddy that's been sitting off the canyon corner all month is still in position, pinching the shelf edge and stacking a clean break where the bluer, warmer water — pushing into the high 70s on the surface — runs up against the cooler green shelf water. That seam is exactly where the bait wants to ride, and exactly where we found feathers of bird activity working the edge around midday. We pulled a mixed spread — green-and-yellow Ilanders over horse ballyhoo on the long riggers, a naked cedar plug in the shotgun, and a small spreader bar down the middle — and picked up three yellowfin in the 35-to-50-pound class right on that thermal line, plus a mahi that came up wild on a teaser and got the naked bait treatment before it ate. We also had a white marlin come tight to the long corner bait, jumped twice, and threw the hook before we could get a pitch bait in front of him — no shot at a release flag, but a good sign of what's building out there.

That's the pattern right now, and it's honestly right on the seasonal clock. We said a week back that the marlin numbers would keep building through August as the canyon warms and the bait tightens up on the edges, and that the yellowfin would stay steady rather than spectacular — holding the temperature break rather than blowing up in one spot. That's exactly what's playing out. Nobody's loading the box on tuna right now, but the fish are there consistently enough that a well-run troll day is putting meat in the fish box, and the marlin shots are becoming a real part of the day instead of a bonus.

Night action off Wilmington has also picked up for the deep-drop guys. A couple of boats working the true canyon depths — 700 to 900 fathoms off the drop past the 38°30' line — have been coming back with bigeye mixed into the tilefish catches on squid strips and glow-bead rigs, fished slow on electric reels after dark. That's not an everyday bite, but when the current's right and the moon isn't blowing out the drift too hard, it's worth the extra fuel to stay out past sundown rather than run home empty on the troll.

Wahoo have been a wildcard. We haven't targeted them hard, but two high-speed strikes on a black-and-purple Braid Marauder run at 12 knots down the wall suggest they're starting to show along the drop-off, which tracks with what we'd expect for mid-August as the water continues to warm and hold. If I had a day dedicated just to wahoo, I'd run that same wall at first light before the sun gets high, when they seem to be feeding closer to the surface.

Chunking is still viable, but I'd treat it as a Plan B rather than the primary play this week. If the troll bite goes quiet — which it can, especially through the heat of midday when the fish seem to sink — sliding into a drift over the canyon's inshore structure with butterflied bunker and a slow chunk line can still pull a yellowfin or two up, especially on the last two hours of daylight when the current eases. But right now, with the eddy holding position and the marlin starting to show consistently, trolling the edge is where I'm putting my time and fuel.

The moon just came off full, so the tidal push out here has been strong, which tends to sharpen the bite windows at dawn and again in the evening rather than spreading fish out evenly through the day. Over the next few days I'd expect that to ease back toward a more standard rhythm, which usually means a longer, steadier midday window rather than two short sharp ones. If the eddy holds its position through the weekend — and there's no strong sign yet that it's sliding — I'd keep running the same stretch of the east wall and expect the white marlin numbers to keep building as we get deeper into August. If it starts to slide east or the temperature break softens, I'd shift effort south toward the Baltimore Canyon corner and reassess from there. Either way, I wouldn't burn the fuel to sit and chunk blind this week — not with a bite this dependent on finding the right water first.
